claims.text: The equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy contains chemically modulated mesoscopic domains after thermomechanical processing.
The mesoscopic domains represent local chemical ordering or chemical short-range order.
The mesoscopic domains are strong obstacles to dislocation motion.
Cr and Mn are involved in forming the mesoscopic domains in Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni.
Equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets lacking one or more critical elements such as Cr or Mn form fewer or smaller ordered domains than the quinary alloy.
The quinary alloy has enhanced strain hardening because its ordered domains impede dislocations.
The quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys can all be prepared as single-phase FCC materials using identical thermomechanical processing.
Synchrotron small-angle diffraction can detect the mesoscopic domains in single-phase Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni.
Plastic deformation deforms, shrinks, and ultimately destroys the mesoscopic domains in Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni.
Destruction of the mesoscopic domains during plastic deformation decreases electrical resistivity, producing the K-effect.
Multi-element interactions in the quinary alloy promote mesoscale chemical ordering.
Fewer or smaller domains in the lower-constituent alloys cause less dislocation obstruction.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys will have lower strain-hardening rates.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys will exhibit smaller electrical-resistivity changes during plastic deformation.
Synchrotron small-angle diffraction will show reduced intensity or no mesoscopic-domain signal in the quaternary and ternary alloys.
The quinary baseline has pronounced mesoscopic domains that correlate with enhanced mechanical resistance during deformation.
The proposed mechanism applies only to comparably processed, single-phase FCC alloys under dislocation-dominated plasticity rather than twinning or phase transformation.
Differences in grain size, residual stress, or nanoprecipitation could also contribute to the mechanical-property differences.
A lack of greater domain prevalence in the quinary alloy, or a lack of correlation between domains and mechanical or resistivity responses, would falsify the hypothesis.
